extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students studying algebraic topology
extracted.subtask_description: Computing homology of CW complexes using degree calculations, cellular chain complexes, and Mayer–Vietoris; includes constructions (maps of given degree, Moore spaces, lens spaces) and algebraic consequences (Euler characteristic, splitting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree equals sum of local degrees (Proposition 2.30)
rubrics_metrics.description: deg f = Σ_i deg f||x_i (the degree of a map equals the sum of the local degrees at the points of a regular value's preimage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via excision and identification of H_n(Ui, Ui − xi) summands ≈ Z. Explanation: identify outer groups with Z, use commutativity of diagrams to see middle map sends generator to local degrees, then sum. Use to reduce global degree computations to local computations; applied e.g. to maps S^n→S^n that send one point from each of k disjoint balls to a value so local degrees ±1 give global degree ±k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing maps S^n→S^n of prescribed degree (Example 2.31 & 2.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce maps with any given degree by collapsing complements of disjoint balls and using quotient/projection maps; z↦z^k on S^1 has degree k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: collapse complement of k disjoint open balls in S^n to a point (quotient q), then project the wedge of k spheres to one sphere (p) and compose f = p q. Local degrees at chosen points are ±1 (homeomorphism near each point); adjust signs by precomposing with reflections. For S^1, z↦z^k has k preimages with local degree +1 (or use reflection for negative k). Suspension preserves degree (see next entry) so repeated suspension gives higher-dimensional examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension preserves degree (Proposition 2.33)
rubrics_metrics.description: deg S f = deg f for the suspension Sf : S^{n+1} → S^{n+1} of f : S^n → S^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via cone CS^n, induced map on pair (CS^n, S^n), and naturality of boundary maps in long exact sequences. Consequence: local degree of suspension at poles equals global degree; hence local degrees in dimensions ≥2 can realize any integer by suspending S^1 examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology of skeleta (Lemma 2.34)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a CW complex X: (a) H_k(X^n, X^{n-1}) = 0 for k ≠ n and is free abelian for k = n with basis corresponding to n-cells. (b) H_k(X^n) = 0 for k > n (so if X finite-dimensional, H_k(X)=0 for k>dim X). (c) Inclusion-induced H_k(X^n)→H_k(X) is an isomorphism for k < n and surjective for k = n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments use that X^n/X^{n-1} is a wedge of n-spheres and long exact sequences of pairs; for infinite-dimensional X use mapping telescope or chain-level compactness (chains meet only finitely many cells). Practical use: reduce homology computations to finite skeleta, and reason about vanishing homology in high degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellular chain complex and equality with singular homology (Theorem 2.35)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cellular chain complex (with C_n = H_n(X^n, X^{n-1}) free on n-cells and differentials d_n) computes H_n(X): H^{CW}_n(X) ≈ H_n(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct chain complex from long exact sequences of pairs (X^{n}, X^{n-1}) with differentials d_n = j_n ∂_{n+1}. Show H_n(X) ≅ Ker d_n / Im d_{n+1}. Consequences: drastically simpler homology computations for CW complexes; use cellular boundary formula to compute differentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellular Boundary Formula
rubrics_metrics.description: For an n-cell e^α_n with characteristic/attaching maps, d_n(e^α_n) = Σ_β d_{αβ} e^{β}_{n-1}, where d_{αβ} is the degree of the composition ∂D^n_α → X^{n-1} → X^{n-1}/X^{n-2} → S^{n-1} projecting to the β summand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute d_{αβ} by collapsing complement of e^{β}_{n-1} to a point and taking degree of the resulting map S^{n-1}→S^{n-1}. Only finitely many β occur because the attaching map has compact image meeting finitely many (n−1)-cells. Diagrammatic derivation given; used in examples (surfaces, RP^n, lens spaces, torus, Klein bottle) to compute matrix entries of differentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate consequences of cellular homology (three facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) If X has no n-cells then H_n(X)=0. (ii) If X has k n-cells then H_n(X) is generated by at most k elements. (iii) If X has no two cells in adjacent dimensions then H_n(X) is free abelian on the n-cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These follow because C_n ≅ Z^{#n-cells} and differentials vanish or have rank limited by numbers of cells; use Ker d_n / Im d_{n+1} arguments. Apply to examples like CP^n, S^n×S^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orientability detected by top homology
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed connected n-manifold M, H_n(M) ≈ Z if M is orientable and 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from cellular homology and will be proved in later theorem (Theorem 3.26 as referenced). Use cellular computations of top cellular boundary map to see whether top-dimensional class survives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute differentials via local degree parity (RP^n example)
rubrics_metrics.description: In RP^n with one cell e^k in each k≤n, the attaching map for e^k is the 2-sheeted covering ϕ: S^{k-1}→RP^{k-1}, and the composition qϕ has degree 1 + (−1)^k, so d_k is 0 for k odd and multiplication by 2 for k even.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequent cellular chain complex alternates differentials 0 and ×2, giving explicit homology groups H_k(RP^n) (Z for k=0 and top when n odd, Z_2 for odd k with 0<k<n, etc.). Use antipodal map degree (−1)^k in computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lens spaces CW structure and alternating boundary maps
rubrics_metrics.description: For lens space L_m(ℓ_1,…,ℓ_n) there is a CW structure with one cell in each dimension ≤2n−1; the cellular boundary maps alternate between 0 and multiplication by m, giving H_k(L) = Z for k=0,2n−1; Z_m for odd 0<k<2n−1; 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses subdividing a circle in last C-factor into m vertices and building balls B^{2n−1}_j whose faces are identified cyclically by rotation ρ. Compute degrees of identifications (reflections give degree −1, rotations degree +1) to determine differentials. Infinite-dimensional limit L_m(…) gives K(Z_m,1) with Z_m in each odd dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of Moore spaces M(G,n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given abelian group G and n≥1, construct CW complex X with H_n(X) ≈ G and H_i(X)=0 for i≠n (and simply-connected if n>1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: take X^n = wedge sum of S^n's so H_n(X^n) ≅ free abelian F surjecting onto G. Let K = ker(F→G) (free), choose bases and attach (n+1)-cells via maps whose degrees realize the relations (d_{βα}) so differential d_{n+1}: Z^{#(n+1)-cells}=K → F includes K as subgroup; quotient gives H_n ≅ G. Use Example 2.31 construction of maps S^n→S^n of prescribed degree to build attaching maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler characteristic equals alternating sum of homology ranks (Theorem 2.44)
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite CW complex X, χ(X) = Σ_n (−1)^n c_n = Σ_n (−1)^n rank H_n(X), so χ depends only on homotopy type and not on CW structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic proof: express chain groups C_n as finitely generated abelian groups, relate ranks via short exact sequences Zn→Cn→Bn−1 and Bn→Zn→Hn, substitute and sum with alternating signs. Use to distinguish surfaces and other spaces by Euler characteristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Splitting Lemma and applications to retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Short exact sequence 0→A→B→C→0 of abelian groups splits iff (a) there is p:B→A with p i = id, (b) there is s:C→B with j s = id, iff (c) B ≅ A⊕C. A retraction r:X→A induces split exact sequences on homology giving H_n(X) ≅ H_n(A) ⊕ H_n(X,A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use splitting to deduce impossibility of certain retractions (e.g., no retraction D^n→S^{n−1} by homology splitting obstruction; mapping cylinder of degree m>1 does not retract onto domain since Z ≄ Z⊕Z_m). Remarks about nonabelian case: (b) weaker than (a) and (c); splitting means semidirect product in nonabelian context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology of groups and torsion obstruction (Proposition 2.45)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a finite-dimensional CW complex X is a K(G,1), then G = π_1(X) must be torsionfree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: torsion subgroup Z_m would give cover K(Z_m,1) that is finite-dimensional and thus would have homology nonzero only in finitely many dimensions, contradicting known H_n(Z_m) ≠ 0 for infinitely many n (Z_m appears in infinitely many odd degrees). Apply to rule out K(G,1) finite-dimensional for groups with torsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayer–Vietoris long exact sequence and explicit boundary map
rubrics_metrics.description: For X = int(A) ∪ int(B), there is a long exact Mayer–Vietoris sequence ··· → H_n(A∩B) → H_n(A)⊕H_n(B) → H_n(X) ∂→ H_{n−1}(A∩B) → ···. The boundary ∂: H_n(X)→H_{n−1}(A∩B) is represented by decomposing a cycle z as x+y with x∈C_n(A), y∈C_n(B); then ∂α is represented by ∂x = −∂y in A∩B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive from short exact sequence of chain complexes 0→C_*(A∩B) → C_*(A)⊕C_*(B) → C_*(A+B) → 0 with maps ϕ(x)=(x,−x), ψ(x,y)=x+y and use Proposition 2.21 to identify C_*(A+B)→C_*(X) on homology. Use barycentric subdivision to arrange cycles as sums in A and B. Applications: compute homology of spheres by splitting into hemispheres, compute Klein bottle via decomposition into Möbius bands, and inductive proofs.
